gapTheirs: B's stems straddle the pixel grid where A's snap to it: the 'b' of "bullet" in B is 3 solid columns fringed on BOTH sides (x92 at mean 91, x96 at mean 167), while A's is flush-left solid at x94–96 with a single fringe column. Global fringe/solid is 0.415 vs A's 0.406, and B's x-height is 22px vs A's 23px at an identical 25.5px advance — smaller type, softer edges, same measure.
verdict: These are the same palette twice: paper #F7F7F7, ink #191919, 16.41:1, zero chroma anywhere, and markers that land at identical ink mass on both sides (bullet 10863 vs 11113, ordered 46648 vs 47257). Only 5.7% of pixels differ at all, and that is scale drift — A renders 1.5% larger, nothing more. Whoever built these did not design two grounds; they rendered one ground twice and let the rasteriser decide the difference. A wins because its stems sit on whole pixels and its x-height is a pixel taller, which is a rendering accident, not a decision — and neither image shows a dark state at all, so half the thing I was asked to judge was never put in front of me.

states.name: dark
states.gap: Ragged marker column: A's four mark kinds start at x=41 (`>`), 44 (`-`), 40 (`1`), 44 (`-`) — a 4px left rag across the mark set, versus B's 40/43/40/43 = 3px. A's larger type inflates the side-bearing spread, so the marker edge wanders ~1px more than B's before the words even begin.
states.gapTheirs: The `-` marker is drawn 5px thick against a 4px body stem (1.25x), while A's dash is 4px against a 4px stem (1.00x). B's type is 1.6% *smaller* than A's (x-height 21px vs 22px, advance 26.3 vs 26.7 px/char) yet its bullet and task dashes render heavier, so on two of four lines the mark blooms louder than the word it marks.
states.verdict: These are near-clones: same #1A1A1A paper, same #CCCCCC ink, same 10.8:1 contrast, same ~1.66 leading ratio, and both correctly rest every marker at the body's own ink rather than greying it out. The split is the dash. B renders `-` at 5px against its own 4px stems, so the bullet and the task box's leading dash sit fractionally bolder than 'bullet item' and 'task not done' — the eye catches on the mark instead of running past it, which is the one thing a mark at body ink is supposed to prevent. A holds the dash at exactly stem weight and sets the type 5% larger for it; B's is a hinting accident that a typographer will see on every list line for the length of the piece.
secondary: Paper is bit-identical in both: flat #1A1A1A, min=max at every sampled row, no gradient, vignette or banding
Both crops show only the dark state — no light palette is visible in either image, so half the brief's subject is unjudgeable from what was supplied
Neither draws a blockquote rule, gutter tint, or indent for the `>` line; the quote is distinguished by the character alone in both
Task box is a literal `[ ]` in both with no box affordance, hit target, or checked-state hint visible
No caret is visible in either image, so caret weight could not be compared
Right/left margin asymmetry favours A: ink runs 41-528 (72px right vs 41px left, 31px imbalance) versus B's 40-520 (80px vs 40px, 40px imbalance)
Marker vertical placement is equally correct in both: `>` and `-` centres sit 2px above x-height centre in each
Overall pixel difference is only 4.6% (AE 10594/228000), almost all of it the 1.6% type-scale offset

states.name: dark-bars
states.gap: Tighter leading: body line pitch 74px vs B's 76px (37 vs 38 CSS px at 2x), ≈1.71 vs ≈1.78 against a ~21.5px body — and 10px (5 CSS px) less air above the H1 (first paragraph top at y=380 vs 390). Over a 6-line paragraph that is a full 12px of lost breathing room; the block reads a shade more packed than B's.
states.gapTheirs: Every marker is demoted to a dim tier instead of resting at the body's ink: `#`, `##`, `*` and `**` all peak at 99/255 (#636363) against #1A1A1A paper — 2.9:1 contrast — while the words they mark sit at 204/255 (#CCCCCC), 10.8:1. A does not demote them: its markers measure 204 exactly like the prose. B compounds it by setting the markers inline rather than hanging them, so the left edge splits into three columns — body text at x=622, H1 text at 673, H2 text at 697 (a 51px and 75px step) — where A hangs `#` at 570 and `##` at 544 and keeps body, H1 and H2 all flush at 622.
states.verdict: The two grounds are the same decision — #1A1A1A paper, #CCCCCC ink, a 3px #00BFFF caret spanning the full line box, a 32px title bar and 26px stats bar with the same #7E7E7E labels under #BDBDBD numbers and the same 1px hairline at y=1748 — so this comes down entirely to how the marks sit on it, and B blinks. Dropping `#` and `**` to #636363 is a designer deciding the writer's own syntax is an embarrassment to be hidden; at 2.9:1 you cannot see at a glance whether you typed one asterisk or two, which is exactly when you need to. Then B refuses to hang them, so the H1 and H2 titles float 51 and 75 pixels right of the paragraph edge and the page has no left edge at all — three ragged starts down one column. A's slightly tighter leading is a real loss and you feel it in the long paragraph, but I would take 2px of leading over a page that can't hold a straight margin or show me what I wrote.
